title: The exit code that never comes
spec: M08 · one PR-review job, three headless invocations
intro: A pipeline needs three things from a tool: run without a TTY, emit something parseable, exit with a code. Two of these tools give you all three. The third gives you none — and the reason is worth more than the verdict.

provenance.source: the three arms are this module's own captured headless invocations, workflow YAML and cost figures, replayed as one pipeline run

foot: The complete workflow YAML for both working arms is in the tabs above; the fifteen-row feature matrix follows in #comparison-matrix.

steps.title: The job: review every PR before a human opens it
narrative: The workflow triggers on pull_request: [opened, synchronize], checks out with fetch-depth: 0 so git diff works, and needs pull-requests: write to post. Everything after that is the tool's problem.

CI asks for three things and does not negotiate. No TTY: nothing may block on a prompt, because there is no keyboard attached. Parseable output: a later step has to turn the answer into a comment body. An exit code: the runner decides pass or fail from the number the process returns, and nothing else.
Score each arm on those three, not on how good the review reads. A brilliant reviewer that hangs waiting for input fails the pipeline exactly as hard as a broken one.
steps.youDo: Write the three invocations down side by side before running anything — the flags alone tell you most of the answer.

terminal.text: git diff origin/main...HEAD > pr_diff.txt   # 3 files, ~400 lines

cells: a blocked prompt is a job that times out at the step limit
the next step has to build a comment body out of it
0 or non-zero is the only signal the runner reads

steps.title: claude -p — print mode was built for this
narrative: -p is short for --print: one prompt in, the full response out, process exits. No REPL is opened. Add --output-format json and the result comes back as a parseable object rather than prose you have to scrape; pipe the diff in on stdin and the whole review is one line of shell.

The official anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 does the rest — installs the CLI, injects the key, fetches the PR diff, calls print mode, and posts the result as a review comment in a single step. It can request changes (blocking merge) or just comment. Setup is genuinely a ten-minute job.

The honest cost line: a three-file, ~400-line diff runs about 2,000 input and 500 output tokens, roughly $0.0135 per PR — and about $0.003–0.006 once prompt caching is configured for the system prompt. That is per-run money, which scales with your PR volume rather than sitting flat. Note too that the unattended-write flag here is --dangerously-skip-permissions: a blunter instrument than the other arm's, named to make you think twice.
steps.youDo: Run it locally first: git diff HEAD~1 | claude -p "Review this diff for security issues" --output-format json, then echo $?.

terminal.text: git diff HEAD~1 | claude -p "Review this diff for security issues. Output as JSON with fields: severity, files_affected, recommendation" --output-format json
review posted to PR #418 · runner step green

view.note: No TTY needed, JSON parsed, exit code honoured, comment posted by the official Action. Cost is per-token and scales with volume — a feature if you want quality on high-stakes diffs, a line item if you review every commit on every branch.

steps.title: gemini -p --no-interactive --yolo — the same job for nothing
narrative: --no-interactive exists specifically so the REPL never opens; --yolo skips every confirmation, which is what unattended file writes require. The name is deliberately dramatic and you should read it that way — in CI it is correct, on your laptop it is a loaded gun.

The economics are the story. The free tier is 60 requests a minute and 1,500 a day, which covers a five-developer team doing five PRs each without spending a cent. Past that, gemini-2.0-flash on the paid API is roughly $0.075 per million input tokens — about $0.0001 per PR review. Against $0.0135 that is two orders of magnitude, on the same job.

Two things it does not hand you. The free tier is per account, so every repo you point at it shares one budget — high-frequency triggers on every commit to every branch is where it breaks, not normal PR traffic. And comment posting is not built in: the official google-github-actions/run-gemini-cli@v1 gives you steps.gemini.outputs.response, and you wire it to the PR yourself through actions/github-script@v7. One extra step, but it is a step the other arm did not need.
steps.youDo: Cap CI cost at zero on purpose: add model: gemini-2.0-flash to the Action and watch the quota, not the invoice.

terminal.text: gemini -p "Review this PR diff as a senior engineer" --model gemini-2.0-flash --no-interactive --yolo --output-format json
exit 0  ·  free tier: 60 req/min, 1,500/day  ·  paid Flash ≈$0.0001/PR
review posted to PR #418 · runner step green

view.note: Cost is not the only axis and this module does not pretend it is: pick Claude Code where review quality on a security-sensitive diff is worth more than the difference, pick Gemini CLI where the volume is high and the stakes are ordinary. Plenty of teams run both — Flash for changelogs and issue labels, Claude for architecture changes.

steps.title: gh copilot suggest — the prompt that never gets answered
narrative: The third arm fails on requirement one and never reaches the others. gh copilot always asks "Would you like to run this command?", and there is no --yes flag to bypass it. In a runner with no TTY the process does not return a useful code — it sits on a prompt nobody can answer until the step times out.

Even if it did return, there is nothing to post. It cannot read a diff, reason across files, or emit structured JSON — it emits one shell command in a fixed format. There is no official Action for autonomous review, and Copilot Workspace, which does create branches and PRs, is a web preview that is not driven by this CLI at all.

None of that is a defect, and the module's own recommendation follows from it: use each tool for its surface. gh copilot suggest -t shell "compress all log files older than 30 days" returns a correct find … -exec gzip one-liner instantly — genuinely useful in a maintenance job you wrote and read yourself — and GitHub Copilot remains the market leader in the editor, where most of a developer's day happens. If you pay for Copilot Business, keep it and add one of the other two to the pipeline. Do not force gh copilot into a role it was never built for.
steps.youDo: Prove the blocker yourself: run gh copilot suggest -t shell "…" in a script with stdin closed, then check $?.

terminal.text: gh copilot suggest -t shell "review the PR diff and post a comment"
? Would you like to run this command? (yes/no)   ← no --yes flag exists
no TTY in the runner · nothing answers the prompt · step times out
gh copilot suggest -t shell "compress all log files older than 30 days"

view.text: "Three very different stories" is exact: two tools were designed for the assembly line and one was designed for a person standing at a terminal. The matrix that follows will show Copilot CLI missing nearly every automation row — read those blanks as the product boundary, not as a scoreboard. The decision this walkthrough should settle is not which tool is best, it is which of the two working arms goes in your pipeline: quality-first on per-token cost, or free-tier-first with one extra wiring step. Running both is a defensible third answer.
